en: The Bodhisattva-prātimokṣa Sūtra. Om, homage to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas!
And as for those three aggregates of ethical discipline (śīlaskandha) of the Bodhisattvas which have been taught:

One who, whether a householder or one who has gone forth, desires to train in the morality of restraint (*saṃvara-śīla*), the morality of gathering virtuous qualities (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and the morality of acting for the welfare of sentient beings (*sattvārthakriyā-śīla*), and who has made the vow for unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, should prostrate at the feet of a fellow-practitioner Bodhisattva— who is a great treasury of merit and capable of communicating through speech and grasping the meaning— and make a formal request.
"O son of good family, O venerable one, O Bhadanta, I desire to receive from you the undertaking of the bodhisattva vow of ethical discipline.
Therefore, please deign, out of compassion for me, to grant it and to listen to my request for a short while, without hindrance."

Having thus requested three times, and having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, he should pay homage to the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present, as well as to the Bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages, throughout the ten directions; bringing their virtues to mind,
generating a profound and intense clarity of heart, and remaining either with his knees bent low or squatting, he [should look upon] the image of the Tathāgata.
Having established [the preceptor] before him, having honored him, and having placed him at the forefront, he should be addressed thus:
"Noble son, Venerable One, or Bhadanta, please grant me the undertaking of the bodhisattva vow of ethical discipline.
Then, having established one-pointed mindfulness, he should cultivate clarity of mind itself.
"Before long, I shall attain an inexhaustible, immeasurable, and unsurpassed great treasury of merit.
While reflecting on this very meaning, he should remain silent.
Then, that wise bodhisattva should address that bodhisattva who has so practiced, whether he is standing or sitting, with an undistracted mind, as follows:
"Listen, O son of good family [or] venerable one, [addressed as] 'Noble One' or 'Venerable Sir': you are a bodhisattva who has made the vow for awakening.
Therefore, you must respond, 'So be it.
He, moreover, should be addressed further as follows:"

"Do you, O son of good family named [so-and-so], Venerable One, or Bhadanta, accept from me all the bodhisattva training rules and the entire bodhisattva morality—the morality of restraint, the morality of gathering virtuous qualities, and the morality of acting for the benefit of sentient beings—which was the morality of the bodhisattvas of the past? "I do. "Then, O son of good family, you are a bodhisattva who has made the vow for awakening."
And those training rules,
whatever morality will belong to future bodhisattvas;
and those training rules, whatever morality currently belongs to the bodhisattvas in the ten directions at present.
And in those training rules and those ethical precepts in which all bodhisattvas of the past have trained,
all bodhisattvas of the future will train,
and all bodhisattvas of the present are training.
He should respond, "I accept," three times in this manner.

May the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the Bodhisattvas assembled from the world-systems of the ten directions attend to me! May the Master [whose name is] so-and-so attend to me: whatever harm I have done, caused others to do, or rejoiced in, by means of body, speech, or mind—whether directed toward the Buddhas, the Bodhisattvas, my parents, or other sentient beings—in this life or in other lives.

Or, having gathered all that together into one, having condensed it, rolled it into a single mass, and weighed it, I confess it before all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and my teacher with the foremost and most excellent confession; knowing and remembering it, I do not conceal it. Thus three times.

I, who am thus named and have thus confessed my transgressions, from this day forward until I sit at the seat of enlightenment, go for refuge to the Buddha, the Blessed One, the Greatly Compassionate One, the All-Knowing, the All-Seeing, who has transcended all enmity and fear, the Great Being with an indestructible body, the unsurpassed body, the Dharma-body— the foremost among two-legged beings.

I, [name], having thus confessed my transgression, from this day forward until I sit at the seat of enlightenment, go for refuge to the Dharma—the peaceful, the most excellent among those free from passion. I, [name], having thus confessed my transgression, from this day forward until I sit at the seat of enlightenment, go for refuge to the Sangha of irreversible Bodhisattvas—the best among assemblies.
Thus three times.

I, who am thus named, having confessed my transgressions in this manner and having gone for refuge to the Three Jewels, for the sake of delivering and uplifting the infinite realm of sentient beings, for their protection from the suffering of *saṃsāra*, and for establishing them in the unsurpassed knowledge of the Omniscient One—

just as those Bodhisattvas of the past, future, and present, having generated the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*), have attained, will attain, and are attaining Buddhahood; and just as all Buddhas, by means of unobstructed Buddha-knowledge and the Buddha-eye, know and see, and just as they authorize the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) of all phenomena.

By that rite, I, [name], in the presence of the teacher named [name] and before all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, generate the mind set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Three times I do this. And I dedicate this root of merit born from the confession of transgressions, the going for refuge in the three jewels, and the generation of the bodhicitta toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment, so that I may be a protection in a world that is without refuge, without shelter, without final resort, and without island.
May I become a refuge, a shelter, a final resort, and an island;
and having crossed over from the ocean of existence myself, may I ferry all sentient beings across.
May I lead those who have not yet attained parinirvāṇa to parinirvāṇa through the unobstructed parinirvāṇa of the dharmadhātu.
May I cause those who have not found rest to find rest. (Three times.)

I, who am thus named and have thus generated the thought of awakening, accept the infinite realm of sentient beings as being equivalent to my mother, father, sister, brother, son, daughter, or any other relative or kinsman.
Having accepted them, I shall plant roots of merit according to my capacity, according to my strength, and according to my knowledge.
From this moment forth, whatever gift I shall give, whatever morality I shall maintain, and whatever patience I shall cultivate, I shall apply myself with vigor.
I shall enter meditative absorption after having investigated with wisdom, or I shall train in skillful means for the sake, benefit, and happiness of all sentient beings.
And with reference to supreme perfect enlightenment, I follow the example of those Bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages, who possess great compassion, and who have entered the Mahāyāna.
Having followed their example, may the Teacher accept me from this moment on as a Bodhisattva, saying, "This one is a Bodhisattva. [Recite this] three times.

Then, in front of that image, having prostrated at the feet of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas dwelling, remaining, and staying in the ten directions, and having performed the *sāmicī* gesture, he should announce as follows:
"By this Bodhisattva of such-and-such a name, from me, a Bodhisattva of such-and-such a name, the undertaking of the Bodhisattva ethical restraint has been accepted up to three times.
I, the Bodhisattva of such-and-such a name, knowing myself to be a witness for this Bodhisattva of such-and-such a name..."

I proclaim this undertaking of the bodhisattva vow of ethical discipline throughout all world systems, infinite and boundless in the ten directions, for all noble beings— even those who are out of my sight— and for all sentient beings whose minds are beyond my perception. Thus, three times.

Furthermore, immediately after the completion of the ritual for undertaking the restraint of ethical discipline (*śīlasaṃvara*), it is indeed the nature of things (*dharmatā*) that in the infinite and boundless world-systems of the ten directions, a corresponding sign appears to the Tathāgatas who are staying, remaining, and maintaining themselves, as well as to the Bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages (*mahābhūmi*), by which they think as follows:
Thus, by the Bodhisattva named [so-and-so], the undertaking of the Bodhisattva’s vow of ethical discipline was received from the presence of the Bodhisattva named [so-and-so].
Thus, first of all, the procedure for undertaking [the precepts] from another has been explained.

If a person endowed with those qualities is not present, then the bodhisattva himself must likewise undertake the vow of the bodhisattva ethical discipline (bodhisattva-śīla-saṃvara) before an image of the Tathāgata,
and it should be done in this manner:
having arranged the upper robe over one shoulder, [he should address] the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present, throughout the ten directions.

Having paid homage to the Bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages (*mahābhūmi*), and having placed his right knee upon the ground or sitting in a squatting posture, he should speak these words:
"I, [name], inform all the Tathāgatas and the Bodhisattvas who have entered the great stages in the ten directions."
In their presence, I undertake all the training precepts of a bodhisattva and the entire morality of a bodhisattva—beginning with "the morality which...

and so forth, as before, up to "a bodhisattva is called a bodhisattva. This is the formal declaration: "From this moment on, may the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and the bodhisattvas hold me [as such]. 0.
